newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian children free pigeons at peace rally.
newsitem.headline: Albanian children free pigeons at peace rally.

text.p: Albanian children held a peace rally with balloons and flowers on Saturday and freed two pigeons to urge adults to put down their guns after an insurrection across the Balkan state last month.

The U.N. Children's Fund UNICEF, which organised the rally attended by about 1,000 children and adults in Tirana's main Skanderbeg Square, said several children have been killed and 150 injured in the violence.

"Please put down your guns. They only bring mothers' tears, death and destruction," one girl told the crowd in bright sunshine in front of the white Palace of Culture, built under former communist rule and flanked by 12 Albanian flags.
"Why did you give us life, to kill us later? We want to hug you but you smell of gunpowder," another girl said.
Schools throughout the country have been closed by unrest since last month along with some orphanages and homes for handicapped children. "Children want books, not guns," one banner read.
Lacking white doves, children released one grey and one speckled pigeon as symbols of peace into the square, once dominated by a statue of Stalinist dictator Enver Hoxha who died in 1985.
Education Minister Luan Skuqi said he reckoned that schools might reopen in the second half of April at the earliest.

"In the meantime, we will be sending lessons by television to eliminate the shortcomings of the school system," he told Reuters at the rally. Priority would go to mathematics, physics, chemistry, literature and Albanian language.
"The whole situation is affecting children's lives," said Gianfranco Rotigliano, the UNICEF representative in Albania.
"The schools are closed, children are hanging around in the streets coming across dangerous things -- arms, grenades, explosives -- and they get the feeling that this is life," he said.
Albanian television has repeatedly played programmes warning people not to pick up bits of metal in the street -- even tiny detonators can blow a child's hand off.
In the lawlessness sparked by public anger at the collapse of savings systems this year, military arsenals have been looted. In many areas, grenades and rifles have become playthings.
In a Tirana street last month, passers-by saw a policeman go up to a boy aged about 12 who was waving an assault rifle at shoppers outside a bakery.

Without trying to disarm him, he told the boy it was safer to hold the gun pointing either straight up or down. The boy respond by spraying bullets at the ground near the policeman's feet, a witness said. The policeman ran away.
